newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Vulnerable to PPI surprise.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Vulnerable to PPI surprise.

text.p: A widely held consensus on Wednesday's producer price report could leave the U.S. credit markets vulnerable to a surprise in the inflation data, market analysts said.
Market players are betting the Producer Price Index (PPI) grew 0.3 percent overall in November and 0.2 percent in its core components, which exclude volatile food and energy prices.
Last month the report showed a 0.4 percent gain overall and a 0.3 percent contraction in core.
"If we saw a number much outside (the consensus), it could have a significant impact on the market," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
A small surprise in the core rate, whether higher or lower than expected, could prompt a strong reaction from Treasuries, several analysts agreed. But most saw the greatest risk on the downside.
"We're richly priced," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc. "The market needs good numbers to justify where it is."
Lieberman forecast 0.4 percent PPI growth, with a 0.2 percent gain in core -- projections he called "not quite good numbers."
"I don't think the market will be oblivious to the 0.4, even though the core is pretty good," he explained.
On the flip side, a number that undercut the consensus by one or two tenths, particularly in core, might boost market sentiment, analysts said.
"Even a one-tenth gain (rather than the projected 0.2 percent) would help out," said Resler.
While analysts agreed the PPI report might push the credit markets around, they said the data probably would not dramatically alter the prevailing belief in moderate growth and subdued inflation.
The current trading range on the 30-year bond yield is 6.40 to 6.60 percent and should stay within those bounds through year-end, analysts said.
How the PPI consensus got wound more tightly than usual this time around was anybody's guess, analysts said, suggesting that a long period of disinflation may have prompted a trend-line forecast.
"Inflation has been relatively calm and subdued in the past few months," said Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc.

The market will use PPI as a warm-up for the more closely watched Consumer Price Index, scheduled for release on Thursday and also expected to have risen 0.3 overall and 0.2 percent excluding food and energy.
Although PPI clearly dominates the calendar on Wednesday, a speech by Alfred Broaddus, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, could get some market attention Wednesday morning.
"There could be some negative reaction to Broaddus, because he tends to be on the hawkish side," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at DLJ Securities Inc.
Broaddus is scheduled to speak to the American Furniture Manufacturers Association in Charlotte, N.C., at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
The Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago's Midwest Manufacturing Index for October is scheduled for release at 1100 EST/1600 GMT on Wednesday. The index was unchanged at a revised 129.5 for September.
--N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1868
